claims.text: Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi lowers the stacking-fault energy in FeNiCrMn.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alters short-range chemical order in FeNiCrMn.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes partial-dislocation activity.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes mechanical twinning relative to ordinary dislocation motion.
Local chemical ordering can affect the rate sensitivity and temperature dependence of plastic flow.
Mechanically derived short-range order is linked to dislocations and stacking faults in low-stacking-fault-energy alloys.
The extent of mechanically derived short-range order can depend on loading rate.
Partial-dislocation glide, twinning, and short-range order evolve concurrently in FeNiCrMn under high strain rates and varying temperatures.
As-solidified FeNiCrMn is single-phase FCC under the proposed initial-state conditions.
As-solidified equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is single-phase FCC under the proposed initial-state conditions.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, FeNiCrMn will exhibit more twinning at lower-to-intermediate temperatures and elevated strain rates.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, FeNiCrMn will exhibit stronger strain hardening at lower-to-intermediate temperatures and elevated strain rates.
At higher temperatures, the dynamic-response differences between FeNiCrMn and CoCrFeMnNi will diminish.
Thermally activated deformation processes at higher temperatures overshadow short-range-order effects.
In-situ diffraction, supplemented by electron microscopy, can characterize deformation-induced stacking faults, twinning, dislocation structures, and stacking-fault energy.
The proposed hypothesis applies only while both compared microstructures remain single-phase FCC.
The proposed comparison assumes stable and similar grain sizes and minimal coarse precipitation.
Equivalent partial-dislocation activity, twinning, and short-range-order evolution in the two alloys under matched conditions would refute the proposed mechanism.
